media:group.media:title: 57,470 British Casualties in One Day #shorts
media:group.media:description:

The full war, day by day, on one map: https://youtu.be/i_wtDU2XYxs

entry.title: World War I, Day by Day (1914–1918)

media:group.media:title: World War I, Day by Day (1914–1918)
media:group.media:description:
At 10:59 on 11 November 1918, an American private named Henry Gunther charged a German machine gun, one minute before the war ended. It had begun 1,567 days earlier with a wrong turn in Sarajevo. This is the whole of World War I on one map, day by day: the July Crisis, the Marne, Tannenberg, the race to the sea, the Christmas Truce, gas at Ypres, Gallipoli, the Great Retreat, Verdun, the first day on the Somme, Jutland, Brusilov, the Russian revolutions, Passchendaele, Caporetto, the Spring Offensive, the Hundred Days and the Armistice.
No narration. Just the map, the dates and the music.
Fun fact: Germany made its final payment on bonds linked to World War I on 3 October 2010, 92 years after the Armistice.
0:00 The last minute 1:15 The wrong turn 2:23 The July Crisis 4:32 1914 10:22 1915 17:17 1916 23:02 1917 30:00 1918 37:55 Aftermath
HOW TO READ THE NUMBERS Casualty figures are the ranges given by Wikipedia (World War I casualties and each battle article) and Britannica (US War Department, 1924). Where sources disagree, a range is shown. Front lines join documented towns in the order the front passed through them; they are simplified, not surveyed trench lines.

entry.title: Napoleon's Retreat From Moscow, Day by Day (1812)

media:group.media:title: Napoleon's Retreat From Moscow, Day by Day (1812)
media:group.media:description:
On 19 October 1812, Napoleon marched out of burned Moscow with about 100,000 men. Fifty-six days later, around 10,000 crossed the Niemen out of Russia. This is the whole retreat on one map: Maloyaroslavets, the old Smolensk road, Vyazma, the first blizzard, Krasnoi and Ney's crossing of the frozen Dnieper, the bridges at the Berezina, Napoleon's sledge to Paris and Ney's last stand at Kovno. The blue line gets thinner as the army shrinks, in the spirit of Charles Minard's famous 1869 chart.
Fun fact: the bridges over the Berezina were built by engineers standing up to their shoulders in a freezing river. A sudden thaw had left it unfrozen, so the army could not simply walk across the ice.
0:00 The bridges 0:12 Leaving Moscow 1:26 The old road 2:42 Krasnoi 3:18 The Berezina 4:22 The last cold 5:12 The numbers
HOW TO READ THE NUMBERS "Men under arms" follows Minard's 1869 chart and modern estimates (Wikipedia, Britannica): c. 95,000–110,000 left Moscow; c. 55,000 by Vyazma; c. 49,000 under arms plus c. 40,000 stragglers at the Berezina (after Victor and Oudinot joined); c. 10,000 crossed the Niemen on Minard's chart. Temperatures are Minard's Réaumur readings converted to °C; his dates are approximate. Positions are drawn through documented towns and dates and simplified between them.

entry.title: How Hitler's Army Reached Moscow, Day by Day (1941)

media:group.media:title: How Hitler's Army Reached Moscow, Day by Day (1941)
media:group.media:description:
At 03:15 on 22 June 1941, about 3.8 million Axis soldiers crossed the Soviet border on a front of some 1,800 km. In 163 days they encircled whole armies at Minsk, Smolensk, Kiev and Vyazma, cut off Leningrad and reached Khimki — about 30 km from the Kremlin. Then the mud, the frost and a Soviet counteroffensive stopped them at the gates of Moscow. This is the whole campaign on one map: the front line day by day, hour by hour for the last days before Moscow.
Fun fact: the famous −40 °C "General Frost" is not in the Moscow weather station record. On 5 December 1941, the day the Soviet counteroffensive began, the daily mean was about −24 °C. The temperature strip in the video shows the real station values.
0:00 The longest front 0:44 The cauldrons 2:30 Ukraine 3:25 Leningrad 4:05 The Kiev pocket 5:00 Typhoon 6:30 The gates of Moscow 8:10 5 December 9:00 The numbers
HOW TO READ THE NUMBERS "Front to Moscow" is the distance from Moscow to the nearest point of the front line as drawn (approx.). Prisoner counts are the German figures for the big encirclements, shown with "c."; Soviet archival figures are lower (e.g. Kiev: German claim 665,000, Soviet data c. 452,700 trapped). Front lines are drawn through documented towns and capture dates and simplified between them. Losses 22 June – 5 December 1941: German c. 0.9–1 million casualties (c. 186,000 killed, army medical reports); Soviet c. 4.5 million (Krivosheev); c. 3.35 million Soviet prisoners in 1941, about 2 million of whom were dead by early 1942.

entry.title: How Napoleon Retook France With 1,100 Men, Day by Day (1815)

media:group.media:title: How Napoleon Retook France With 1,100 Men, Day by Day (1815)
media:group.media:description:
On 1 March 1815 Napoleon landed at Golfe-Juan with about 1,100 men. Twenty days later he was back in the Tuileries — and no one had fired a shot at his army. Then all of Europe came for him. This is the whole return, from Elba to St Helena, on one map: day by day for the march on Paris, hour by hour for Waterloo.
Fun fact: the "Hundred Days" were really 110. The phrase comes from the prefect of Paris, Chabrol, welcoming Louis XVIII back on 8 July 1815 — he was counting the King's absence (20 March – 8 July).
The clock on screen slows down for the big moments; the badge shows the date (and the hour at Waterloo).
0:00 Escape from Elba 0:40 The Route Napoléon 1:08 Grenoble and Lyon 1:44 Paris without a battle 2:30 Europe mobilises 3:48 Into Belgium 4:16 Ligny and Quatre Bras 4:44 Storm and retreat 5:30 Waterloo, hour by hour 8:12 Abdication and exile 9:08 The numbers
HOW TO READ THE NUMBERS Army strengths are the most-cited figures; where historians disagree we show "c." and use the middle of the range (e.g. Waterloo: French c.72,000, Wellington c.68,000, Prussians c.45,000–50,000 engaged). Losses accumulate over the day for display; totals are the commonly cited ones (French c.25,000 killed and wounded plus 7,000–10,000 captured; Wellington c.17,000; Prussians c.7,000). The strength of Napoleon's column on the march is a narrative estimate. Unit positions on the battlefield are approximate.
